title: At peace with God
hookLine: dying, asked if he'd made peace with God, he reportedly said he didn't know they had quarreled

lines: I DIDN'T KNOW WE HAD QUARRELED.
cards: A sickroom in Concord. Thoreau is very ill, near the end of his life. A relative asks whether he has made his peace with God, and the story goes that he answered, quietly, that he wasn't aware they had ever quarreled.
One question, one answer. It's a story that gets retold, and it comes to us secondhand. But it sounds like him.
And it opens a real question.

teach.b: First, the question was a kind one. Asking someone near death whether they've made peace with God can be an act of love. The relative isn't the villain here.
Second, the answer. Thoreau doesn't argue about doctrine. He doesn't say yes, and he doesn't say there's no God.
He says, in effect, there was never a fight. Whatever he meant by God, he didn't experience the relationship as broken. A whole outlook, folded into one sentence.
Third, where that outlook shows up in his books.
In Walden he writes, "God himself culminates in the present moment, and will never be more divine in the lapse of all the ages." For Thoreau the sacred wasn't far away and angry.
It was here, in this hour, in the pond and the morning. If you meet God, or whatever you call it, in the present moment, there's nothing to patch up later.
Another reported answer from those last weeks: asked about the next world, he said, one world at a time. Fourth, what to do with this.

Different traditions answer the question of peace with God in their own ways, with confession, repentance, grace, surrender, and they mean deep things by them. Thoreau's line doesn't settle that for anyone.
What it offers is a picture of a man who, at the end, seemed unafraid. Not because he'd won an argument, but because he hadn't been having one.

how: Some readers repeat Thoreau's reported deathbed answer as a picture of calm at the end of life, and pair it with his line in Walden that God culminates in the present moment.

a deathbed prayer asking God to forgive his sins
his promise to rejoin his family's church at last

games.q: you're Thoreau, near the end. someone who loves you asks if you've made your peace with God. what do you say?
o: that you have nothing to say.
that you didn't know you had quarreled.
games.why: the story goes that he answered he wasn't aware they had ever quarreled: no fight, so nothing to patch up.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been quietly at war with: your body, the weather, a noise next door, the pace of your own healing.

Don't try to love it; just see whether, for now, you can stop fighting it and breathe beside it, the way you'd sit beside someone you're no longer arguing with. If you pray, you might bring it to God in your own way.

wordCard.voice: At peace with God. The story of Thoreau, near the end, answering that he didn't know they had ever quarreled. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: no quarrel. Sometimes peace is noticing there was never a fight. Rest easy; more tomorrow.
